extractionNotes: FULL EXTRACTION COMPLETE (Phase 9). All 170 PDF pages read (front matter pages ~1-24 skipped as document-level boilerplate per schema design notes). Final in-body totals: 3 Strands, 8 named Sub-Strands recurring across Years as 21 Sub-Strand year-instances (some Sub-Strands do not recur in every year - see below), 35 Learning Outcomes, 36 Content Standards, 64 Learning Indicators. This differs slightly from the Phase-1 inventory's provisional totals (36 LO / 36 CS / 63 LI) taken from the document's own Scope-and-Sequence summary table (PDF page 23); that table's pdftotext -layout extraction is itself visibly garbled/column-misaligned (confirmed by manual inspection) and is judged unreliable as a cross-check. The in-body Learning Outcome/Content Standard/Learning Indicator content (this file) is treated as authoritative per extraction rules; the 1 LO / 1 LI discrepancy vs. the summary table is recorded here rather than silently reconciled.

Sub-Strand recurrence across years (confirmed by reading the full document body, contradicting parts of the Phase-1 inventory's guesses about WHICH sub-strands skip which years): 'Robots & Society', 'Robot Control Principles', 'Sensors & Actuators' (Strand 1) each recur in Years 1, 2 and 3. 'Digital and Analogue System Design' (Strand 2) recurs in all 3 years (contrary to the garbled summary table appearing to show no Year 3). 'Tools & Apps for Robot Design' (Strand 2) recurs in Years 1-2 only, no Year 3 row exists anywhere in the body. 'Higher Order Design Thinking' (Strand 3) recurs in Years 1-2 only, no Year 3 row exists in the body (this was NOT flagged as missing-Year-3 in the Phase-1 inventory, an additional finding from this full pass). 'Robot Construction' (Strand 3) recurs in all 3 years, with the Year 3 instance's sole Content Standard (3.3.2.CS.1) explicitly prefixed 'Final Year project' in its printed description, matching the inventory's capstone-project note. 'Programming Robots' (Strand 3) recurs in Years 1-2 only; the source PDF's physical content ends (page 170 / printed page 168) partway through 'Robot Construction' Year 3's Teaching and Learning Resources list, confirming no Year 3 'Programming Robots' content exists at all.

Curriculum codes for the Strand/Sub-Strand hierarchy, taken from the in-body 'Strand n. .../Sub-Strand n. ...' headings and their composite codes, differ from this same document's own Phase-1 inventory's provisional placement: 'Higher Order Design Thinking' is coded and headed as Strand 3 Sub-Strand 1 (not Strand 2 Sub-Strand 3 as the inventory guessed), and Strand 3 ('Robot Construction & Programming' / 'Robot Construction and Programming' - both spellings seen, preserved verbatim per year) has exactly 3 Sub-Strands (Higher Order Design Thinking, Robot Construction, Programming Robots) while Strand 2 ('Robot Design Methodologies') has exactly 2 (Digital and Analogue System Design, Tools & Apps for Robot Design). In-body codes are treated as authoritative.

Front matter (PDF pages 1-24): shared SHS boilerplate (SHS Curriculum Overview, Philosophy/Vision/Goal of Robotics, 21st Century Skills, GESI, SEL Five Core Competencies, Learning and Teaching Approaches, UDL, Bloom's/Webb's DoK framework, Curriculum Development Panel, Scope and Sequence table) - not re-extracted per node, per schema Phase 5 design notes. PDF page 3 contains a leftover/garbled title-block artifact from a different subject ('PHYSICAL AND HEALTH EDUCATION...BASIC 7-10') consistent with a shared production template across the SHS PDF batch; not part of Robotics content.

Sub-Strand 1.1.2 'Robot Control Principles', Year One: the source document prints TWO different Content Standards, each with its own two Learning Indicators and two Assessment items, but BOTH are labelled with the identical code '1.1.2.CS.1' ('Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of robot subsystems and their functions.' on pp.33-34 printed, vs. 'Demonstrate knowledge of fundamental control principles in automation and robotics.' on p.35 printed) - each internally reusing LI.1/LI.2 and AS.1/AS.2 as well. Preserved verbatim as printed (both stored, distinguished here by sequence 1 and 2); flagged NEEDS_REVIEW on Sub-Strand 1.1.2 Year One.

Sub-Strand 1.1.2 Year One, first Content Standard (subsystems): the source PDF re-prints the entire Content-Standard/Learning-Indicator-1 table row a second time at the top of the continuation page (printed p.34) as a running table-header/continuation convention when a table row spans a page break (confirmed by comparing single-page extractions of PDF pages 35 and 36). This is a page-layout artifact of the source PDF's table pagination, not duplicate curriculum content; the Learning Indicator's text was recorded once.

learningIndicators.description: Identify both local and global problems that can be fixed using robots and automated systems.

Each member in a group identifies an industry and points out a problem or identifies an opportunity that requires automation or robot integration in the current operational processes of a local industry. Share the identified problem or opportunity with group members. Group should discuss and prioritise the list of problems and opportunities.

learningIndicators.description: Learners should identify, document, and present problems in society and local industries, as well as suggest the role robots can play in solving these problems.
pedagogicalExemplars: Project-Based Learning: For a given local Ghanaian industry, Learners should work in groups to discuss robot-based design ideas that can be used to address the problem or opportunity. The following steps will be a good guide: The group should adopt one of the problems or opportunities and discuss robot-based design ideas that can be used to address the problem or opportunity. Learners Sketch out design ideas on paper and consider local and realistic components that can be sourced and used to implement the various ideas. Group discussion and prioritisation of different concepts and the selection of the best-fit solution. Each group should prepare to share the following with the rest of the class: a. How did the team arrive at the final design solution? b. Is the design realistic and well proportioned? c. How did each team member contribute towards the overall design? d. Do you feel like everyone had an equal opportunity to contribute to the creative process?

learningOutcomes.description: Design and program Finite State Machines

guidance.twentyFirstCenturySkills: Information literacy: Learners are informed as they are guided through the flow of control programs. Critical thinking: Learners use the knowledge in decision-making programs and flow of control programs to create finite-state controls that automate the behaviour of a built robot. Emotional Intelligence: Learners develop the discipline of meeting deadlines and the set project objectives. Collaboration: Learners sit in well-mixed (gender-balanced and culturally diverse) groups and contribute to developing decision-making programs. The right ambience should be created to allow every learner to collaborate with others, building on points raised and putting down their collective observations while amicably resolving issues of differences in opinions. Leadership: As learners sit in groups to brainstorm and develop decision-making programs, they create and share tasks and responsibilities among themselves to achieve set goals for the group. Social Skills: As learners meet and network, they develop social skills

guidance.additionalValuesNote: 1. As facilitators provide resources, they are mindful of biases, stereotypes, and prejudices and place efforts to provide well-balanced examples.
